newsitem.title: FRANCE: Fire damage keeps Channel Tunnel shut another day.
newsitem.headline: Fire damage keeps Channel Tunnel shut another day.

text.p: The French rail authority SNCF advised London-Paris and London-Brussels passengers on Wednesday to delay their travel or make other arrangements as the Channel Tunnel remained shut down for another day due to fire damage.
For those who planned to travel on the crack Eurostar trains on Wednesday, "It would be better to cancel or put off your trip," an SNCF spokesman said.

He said Eurotunnel officials planned to re-evaluate the situation in early afternoon but were likely to resume only limited service even if it was determined that enough progress had been made in repairing the damage from Monday's tunnel fire.

The spokesman estimated that about 8,000 to 10,000 people had expected to travel between London and Paris by Eurostar on Wednesday and another 2,500 between London and Brussels, who would now have to put off their plans or go by ferry or air.
The Anglo-French link could face weeks of disruption after the blaze on a lorry aboard a freight train -- the first major accident since it opened two years ago.
The blaze injured eight people and damaged 600 metres (yards) of the 51-km (32-mile) rail tunnel.
"There is a lot of mess down there," Alain Bertrand, operations director of Eurotunnel SA Plc told Britain's Press Association news agency in Calais.
Repair services worked through the night in an attempt to restore services and repair damaged equipment.

With one of the two main tunnels undamaged, hopes had been high earlier on Tuesday that, a partial service could begin on Wednesday morning. Bertrand said some travellers might be allowed through on Wednesday afternoon "at the very earliest".
When the high-speed trains do start running again, the best the company can hope for is a quarter to a third of normal traffic.

Shuttle services for cars -- which, like trucks, are loaded aboard trains at Calais or Folkestone -- would take second place. The tunnel comprises three parallel tunnels -- two for trains, one for maintenance and emergencies.
The fire started in one of 29 trucks aboard a shuttle train about 18 kms (11 miles) from the French entrance. Some 70 French and British fire-fighters fought all night to control it.

The blaze was a new setback for the troubled Eurotunnel operator which is trying to shake off a record of breakdowns, cost over-runs and debts and recently came close to bankruptcy after restructuring its $15 billion debt.
Eurotunnel has not yet estimated the cost of repairing the damaged rails, electric cables and carriages.
Bertrand said the authorities were attempting to determine whether a lorry's cargo was already smouldering before the freight train entered the tunnel at Calais.
"It might have been that it did not become a big fire until the train was inside the tunnel," he said.

Bertrand insisted that the first inspection of the damage had done nothing to change Eurotunnel's belief that security precautions and evacuation tactics fulfilled the promise of pre-launch exercises.
